frase_gancho.texto: A Chac Mool of gray stone, severe and geometric, in the heart of Michoacán.

puente_narrativo.texto: The Purépecha did not only work stone. Look for a display case with a copper pectoral and small metal bells: the metal that made these artisans famous.

guion_corto.texto: This volcanic stone sculpture, more than a meter long, comes from Ihuatzio, one of the Purépecha cities of Michoacán, and it was made between the years 1350 and 1521. It is a Chac Mool: a man reclining on his back, with his knees bent and his head turned to one side, holding a vessel on his belly. You already saw this figure in the Toltec Hall and in the Maya Hall. Here it is different: it has straight planes, severe lines and very little decoration. The Purépecha took a foreign idea and made it their own. It is a sober, geometric piece, almost modern. It served as an altar for offerings to the gods.

guion_largo.texto:
When something travels, it changes. This piece is the proof. It is the same [Chac Mool](mna_s05_chacmool_tolteca) you saw in Tula and in Chichén Itzá, but carved by Purépecha hands, with a different character.

Compare it in your memory. The one from Tula has volume and ornaments; the one from Chichén, fine attire. This one is dry, geometric, with planes cut almost at right angles. The head is sober, and the body has nothing but the essential. It is another kind of elegance, the elegance of austerity.

You have already seen how the idea traveled from Tula to Yucatán. Here it reaches Michoacán, in the west, and each region adapted it. We do not know how it was transmitted. What we do see is that the Purépecha did not copy: they reinterpreted.

Ihuatzio, it is said, means «place of coyotes». It was one of the three capitals of the Purépecha, along with Tzintzuntzan and Pátzcuaro. According to the Relación de Michoacán, the hero Tariácuri divided the government between his son and his nephews, one in each city. And sculptures of seated coyotes have been found there. The coyote has accompanied you on this tour: the bone from Tequixquiac, the warrior from Tula and now Ihuatzio. An animal that crosses the entire country.

The vessel it holds received offerings. In Purépecha religion, the main god was Curicaueri, the fire, and the altar of the ceremonial plaza was a place of exchange with the sacred. It is thought that this figure was a messenger: it carried the gifts of the nobility to the god.

A small experiment, if no one is nearby: imagine copying its posture. Back to the ground, knees bent, head turned, something heavy on your belly. It is hard to hold for long. It is a posture of waiting, not of rest, and that explains its air of alertness. It measures more than one meter thirty in length, and moving it to the museum was a considerable operation.

Look closely at the stone. Andesite is a very hard volcanic rock. The Purépecha worked it with patience, polishing the surfaces with abrasives and water until they were clean. In the fourteenth century, when it was carved, this people already mastered the working of copper and bronze, but to sculpt they still used stone tools. It is another way to see how much knowledge accumulated in this region.

The Purépecha and the Mexica were rivals, and yet they share this figure: there was also a Chac Mool in the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan. Wars closed borders, but not ideas. Ideas crossed through trade, diplomacy, travelers and artisans.

When the Spaniards arrived, the last Purépecha ruler, Tangáxoan, did not confront them with weapons; he submitted in 1522, and a few years later he was executed by Nuño de Guzmán. The independence that had been so costly to preserve ended without a battle and with an unjust death.

Look again at the turned head. In Tula, in Yucatán and here, the same posture welcomes whoever arrives. It is as if each civilization said the same thing to the visitor with a different accent: «I was waiting for you».

texto: Compare the shape of the head with that of the Chac Mool in the previous halls
Find the circular vessel on the belly
Observe the straight planes of its body: what feeling do they give you?

texto.Origin: Ihuatzio, Michoacán (Ihuatzio archaeological zone, Lake Pátzcuaro basin)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Purépecha were conquered by the Mexica.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They resisted the Mexica and kept their independence until the arrival of the Spaniards.
